title: Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Food and Nutrition Education: State of The Art Review
extended_summary:
This state-of-the-art review examines the role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in food and nutrition education, with particular attention to four dimensions: applications, benefits, challenges, and contributions to personalized learning. The authors ask how GenAI is being used in nutrition education and what its educational value is when compared with conventional, non-AI approaches. The review is framed around conversational AI and large language models such as ChatGPT, especially where they are used to generate educational materials, dietary guidance, quizzes, and feedback.

The paper synthesized nine peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2025 from PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Included evidence covered university teaching, family-oriented nutrition programs, and clinical dietetics/patient education. The populations represented in the underlying studies include undergraduate students and adult users such as parents, caregivers, patients, and nutrition professionals, though the review itself is not a single primary intervention study. The context spans academic settings, online and blended family programs, and clinical nutrition environments.

Across the literature, GenAI was found to be most useful as a supervised adjunct rather than a stand-alone replacement for conventional instruction or professional judgment. Reported advantages included improved readability of learning materials, personalized explanations and quizzes, better learner engagement, and support for nutrition literacy and dietary counseling. However, the review also highlights major limitations, including variable accuracy, gaps in completeness and rigor, language- and prompt-sensitivity, privacy concerns, and the risk of automation bias. The authors conclude that GenAI can strengthen nutrition education when it is expert-reviewed, aligned with professional standards, and integrated with human oversight and digital-literacy support.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed state-of-the-art narrative review with transparent search methods, but it does not present a controlled primary evaluation and includes heterogeneous evidence. The paper is methodologically structured, yet the underlying evidence base is mostly descriptive, cross-sectional, or pilot-level.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests meaningful but still preliminary benefits for engagement, personalization, and scalable nutrition education, without pooled effect sizes or strong causal evidence. Reported impacts are promising but remain largely indirect, short-term, and context-specific.

interventions.use_case: State-of-the-art review of generative AI/chatbots (e.g., ChatGPT, LLMs) used for food and nutrition education, including personalized nutrition advice, tailored quizzes and feedback, readable learning materials, and supervised counseling support in university, family, and clinical dietetics contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, GenAI was described as improving efficiency for educators and clinicians by rapidly generating first-draft learning materials, tailoring quizzes and feedback, and summarizing nutrition information for instruction and counseling. The review reports engagement metrics such as 220,000 website views, >9 million social-media reach, 14,698 chatbot downloads, and >24,000 chatbot responses in the Nutripedia campaign, indicating scalable dissemination rather than a controlled causal effect.
finding.measure: Engagement metrics, chatbot downloads, website views, social-media reach, number of chatbot responses; narrative synthesis of workflow efficiency
finding.study_size: n=9 studies (review); campaign-level metrics reported for one included study

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that GenAI-supported programs improved student engagement and sustained participation, especially when used in supervised or gamified formats. In one included pilot, a gamified chatbot plus weekly seminars improved parental nutrition knowledge and maintained participation, but the paper does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Engagement/participation indicators and perceived engagement in included studies
finding.study_size: n=9 studies (review); pilot sample sizes not reported in the review text

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests GenAI can support critical appraisal and AI literacy when outputs are used as draft material under expert supervision, but it also warns of automation bias, superficial understanding, and overconfidence when tools are used unsupervised. Because the evidence base is heterogeneous and mostly descriptive, the net effect on durable skills is mixed rather than firmly positive.
finding.measure: Narrative assessment of critical appraisal, AI literacy, and automation bias risk

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is governance, professional oversight, privacy, equity, and the need for human-in-the-loop workflows in nutrition education and counseling. The review concludes that GenAI is best used as a supervised adjunct aligned with professional standards, but current evidence also highlights risks related to inequity, misinformation, and role ambiguity.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of governance, oversight, privacy, equity, and professional-role considerations
